Additionally, the RBMLE method has been found to be robust to changes in reward structure, and it can still optimize performance even when the rewards are changed after training. Overall, the proposed RBMLE method provides a way to improve the efficiency of neural contextual agents by optimizing their reward-based performance. Human creativity is characterized by an unparalleled capacity for innovative 
expression through metaphors, which are a fundamental aspect of human language. 
Despite the importance of metaphors, current AI systems struggle to effectively 
capture their linguistic and visual manifestations. This research addresses the 
shortcoming by developing a comprehensive dataset and resource for visual 
metaphors, specifically focusing on the challenges of identifying and analyzing 
metaphor images, which are a major hurdle in the field. Our dataset, MetaCLUE, 
is a large-scale, multi-domain collection of 12,000 visual metaphors that 
includes 9,000 images with detailed annotations for both input and output elements. 
Furthermore, we provide 3,000 samples with complete analysis, including the 
identification of mapping sense and the extraction of conceptual concepts. 
MetaCLUE is a pioneering dataset in the field of visual metaphors, offering a 
comprehensive resource for researchers to advance the field of expression. Our 
analysis and evaluation of the dataset confirm its value in enabling the 
complete automation of metaphor generation. Our ultimate goal is to establish 
MetaCLUE as the standard benchmark for visual metaphor research, driving forward

This paper introduces the concept of the dual measure, a complementary quantity to the primal measure, defined for any convex body in a given space. We demonstrate that this dual measure results in a linear function, and that this function can be utilized to determine the optimal value and dual optimal value of any linear optimization problem. Specifically, we establish that the optimal value of any linear optimization problem is bounded below by the dual measure of the optimal solution and above by the dual measure of the tightest convex shape that encloses the optimal solution. Moreover, we show that the optimal value of any linear optimization problem is bounded below by the dual measure of any point within the feasible region and above by the dual measure of any point outside the feasible region. Our findings are then applied to solve various problems, including the identification of the optimal bounds for the volume of simplices, the determination of the radius of convex polytopes, the identification of the smallest convex polytope that can enclose a given point, and the identification of the largest convex polytope that can enclose a given point. Lastly, we provide examples of calculating the primal and dual measures for specific convex polytopes. The authors also present a comprehensive table summarizing the primal and dual measures for various well-known convex polytopes. Brain tumor segmentation using MRI scans is a crucial step in developing effective treatment plans. The challenge lies in accurately segmenting tumors from the brain, as it is a highly complex task. To address this issue, we propose a novel 3D U-Net-based approach that incorporates contextual information. The approach uses a 3D U-Net to extract tumor features and a 2D CNN to incorporate contextual information. The contextual information is then fed into a 1x1 convolutional layer to generate a probability map. This map is then combined with the UNet features to produce a final segmentation map. To further improve performance, we also incorporate a conditional variance-based skip connection. Our approach was evaluated on the BRATS 2019 dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to other methods. Notably, the use of contextual information resulted in significant improvements, particularly in the tumor core and enhancement segments. The source code for our approach is available on GitHub for public use. Further, we plan to enhance our approach by leveraging attention mechanisms to extract more informative features. The ultimate goal of our research is to develop a robust brain tumor segmentation model that can be seamlessly integrated into clinical settings. Conditional independence relationships are crucial for constructing tree topology models in various fields such as genetics and education. A new method for identifying equivalent nonparametric models based on their tree topologies has been developed, allowing a more efficient comparison of models in certain cases. A key property of tree topology models is that their marginal distributions can be easily calculated using standard techniques. Theoretical findings have been applied to the analysis of data from the US Census to investigate relationships among different variables. Furthermore, research has also been conducted on multivariate tree topology models, which involve multiple outcomes observed at various time points. A sufficient condition for identifying these models has been established, and specific cases have been identified through theoretical and simulation studies. The research also demonstrates how to determine the maximum likelihood estimator for multivariate tree topology models and provides a computationally efficient algorithm for this purpose. Theoretical and simulation results have shown that the performance of the proposed estimator and algorithm is satisfactory, and its accuracy is close to optimal in most cases. The methodology has been successfully applied to the analysis of US Census data, revealing interesting relationships among variables such as education, employment, and income. Recent advancements in reinforcement learning have led to significant breakthroughs in complex tasks, yet tackling challenging problems is still a difficult endeavor. To overcome this challenge, researchers have proposed imitation learning as an alternative approach. Imitation learning mimics expert behavior by learning from a demonstration dataset, but current off-policy methods struggle with aligning policy distributions due to the vast difference between demonstrations and training environments. To address this limitation, we introduce SoftDICE, an innovative imitation learning algorithm that effectively adapts to distribution shifts through a novel combination of density ratio matching and a soft update strategy. By leveraging a soft update policy, SoftDICE achieves superior performance on various tasks, including continuous control and robotic manipulation, even in the presence of significant distribution mismatch. Thorough experiments and theoretical analysis confirm the superiority of SoftDICE, setting a new standard for the field. Finally, the work presents a set of linear equations for describing the coprimeness properties of discrete systems, without assuming coprime components, at a computational cost of O(N^4logN) operations. An example illustrating the application of this theory to discrete systems without irreducibility assumptions is also provided. However, the paper notes that determining the coprimeness characteristic matrix is a computationally challenging problem, specifically an NP-hard problem. Consequently, the authors propose a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for computing this characteristic matrix, and demonstrate its efficacy through numerical examples. Constructive cryptography is a theoretical approach to security, focusing on understanding the underlying security assumptions of cryptographic protocols rather than their implementation weaknesses. We explore and leverage this perspective to develop new cryptographic protocols, specifically by incorporating an interactive setup phase into two fundamental cryptographic protocols. 

Our initial innovation lies in introducing an interactive setup variant of the Learning With Errors protocol, which yields a new constructive approach to key exchange and multi-party computation, featuring the unique property of being post-compromise secure, even achieving the highest level of security known at the time of publication. 

We subsequently develop an interactive setup variant of the Private Information Retrieval protocol, which serves as a foundation for the development of the first updatable encryption scheme, including both a theoretical proof of security and a secure implementation. The results of our work encompass both the theoretical and practical applications of constructive cryptography, including a novel approach to developing more secure systems by reusing keys. Furthermore, our work includes a separate contribution, which is an alternative way of developing updatable encryption, utilizing the Cycles of Permutations framework. 

Notably, while our work focuses on developing new cryptographic protocols, it also highlights the limitations of the Constructive Cryptography approach to security, including a reduction in security levels and the challenges associated with designing protocols that are not of the "black-box" type. The results of our work are intended to spark further discussion and research on the theoretical and practical implications of Constructive Cryptography, including the role of Interactivity in this approach to security.

Estimating brain connectivity from resting fMRI data is a complex task due to its inherent heterogeneity. GANs have become increasingly popular in computer vision for their ability to generate high-quality images, but they are often plagued by mode collapse, which causes the model to fail to produce a diverse range of images, even when given diverse inputs. To address this issue, researchers have developed many different techniques to improve GAN training, but they have not yet been able to fully understand why mode collapse happens, or how to prevent it. To fill this gap, this paper takes a closer look at mode collapse by analyzing how the model's parameters change as it is trained, using a measure called Hessian eigenvalues. By applying this analysis to a variety of GAN architectures, including DCGAN, BigGAN, and StyleGAN, researchers have been able to identify a number of key findings, including the observation that mode collapse is more likely to happen when the model's parameters are concentrated in a small number of dimensions, and when those parameters are not optimized in a way that allows the model to explore its full range of possibilities. These findings suggest that mode collapse is a complex issue, caused by a combination of factors, rather than just one, and are consistent across different types of GAN architectures. As a result, they provide a foundation for future research to build on, and offer new insights into how to improve the performance of GANs. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of Hessian eigenvalues as a diagnostic tool for understanding and preventing mode collapse, and provides a roadmap for future research in this area. All of the code and data used in this study have been made publicly available, allowing others to build on these findings and take GAN research forward. To the best of the researchers' knowledge, this study is the first to analyze mode collapse using Hessian eigenvalues, and is a significant step forward in the field of GAN research. In recent years, network analysis has become a crucial tool for uncovering the intricate structures within complex systems such as social and biological networks. A key focus in this field is the prediction of missing links in a given network, which can provide valuable insights into the underlying structure of the system. This study introduces a novel approach called MultiSAGE, designed to address the challenge of inter-layer link prediction in multi-layer networks. MultiSAGE leverages the concept of a "bottleneck" layer to enhance the embedding capabilities of the widely used node2vec algorithm. By applying node2vec sequentially on each layer of a multi-layer network, which is first represented as a simplified graph structure known as a line graph, MultiSAGE generates a rich feature space that captures the topological characteristics of each individual layer. Our experiments demonstrate that MultiSAGE outperforms existing methods in inter-layer link prediction across a range of multi-layer networks, and also showcases its ability to successfully identify missing nodes in a challenging scenario. Moreover, MultiSAGE has been shown to be a versatile tool that can be applied to a range of network analysis tasks, including the prediction of community structures and the identification of influential nodes. Our research highlights the potential of MultiSAGE as a powerful framework for analyzing and understanding the complex structures of social and biological networks. We develop a new method for estimating functions with significant gradients, 
where a monotone cubic spline approach is applied to a transformed function via maximum likelihood estimation on observed data. Our estimator exhibits optimal convergence rates and we construct a corresponding confidence interval, which we evaluate through simulations and an actual application involving US presidential election results. 

In addition, our analysis includes a simulation study which demonstrates that the cubic spline method outperforms Baskerville's piecewise linear approach, while also allowing for the ability to handle the log-odds transformation's non-differentiability issue that affects the linear approach. This new method enables us to accurately predict probabilities for voting and we find that the actual voting percentage is closely related to the log-odds transformation. Furthermore, our results also reveal the existence of spatial heterogeneity in voting patterns. Crucially, our estimator maintains the monotonicity property, which is a key requirement for the log-odds transformation. 

However, our approach is not limited to this specific application and can be successfully applied to other binary response regression scenarios. While our estimator is grounded in asymptotic normality, the finite sample performance is evaluated through simulation-based Monte Carlo methods. Our methodology is made available for public use on the GitHub platform. Finally, an actual application involving US presidential election results is presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in practice. This note examines the effectiveness of the polar-like decoding method for codes with symmetric properties. It establishes that these decoding algorithms are correct when operating up to half the code's minimum Hamming distance. Moreover, when the polar-like decoder accurately determines half the code's minimum Hamming distance, it can decrypt a codeword's original message with zero error. To illustrate this concept, we analyze the two-codeword set $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]$ and 8-codeword set $[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14]$, and find that their associated symmetric codes yield suboptimal results. To address this issue, we introduce a new construction that generates a linear code from an existing code, and we prove that this method yields a code with a minimum Hamming distance twice that of the original code when the original code has a minimum Hamming distance of at least 3. Furthermore, when the original code has a minimum Hamming distance of at least 3 and is generated by the new construction, we establish that its associated polar-like decoder functions correctly when the decoder operates up to half the code's minimum Hamming distance. In addition, when the decoder accurately determines half the code's minimum Hamming distance, we can decrypt a codeword's original message with zero error. In comparison, we also observe that the suboptimal results obtained from the codes based on the new construction are better than those obtained from the codes based on the symmetric codes of the original code. In addition, we construct a code from the set $[1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 12, 14]$, and we find that its associated polar-like decoder functions correctly when the decoder operates up to half the code's minimum Hamming distance. Recent advancements in vision-language models based on large pre-trained models have achieved exceptional performance in zero-shot image classification tasks. However, their high computational demands and memory requirements are significant drawbacks. To address this issue, we propose a domain prompt method that enables efficient adaptation of these models to unfamiliar domains. By integrating domain-specific prompts, our approach achieves remarkable zero-shot classification performance, while reducing computational costs substantially. Specifically, our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method can replicate the high performance of the full CLIP model, yet can be up to 30 times more computationally efficient. Furthermore, our method can adapt CLIP to new domains with as little as 10% of the original model's parameters, resulting in a 30 times increase in efficiency. Notably, our findings are validated by experiments conducted across various visual recognition tasks, including image classification, object detection, and visual question answering, all of which yielded promising results. A novel dynamic filter is introduced, allowing for the update of its coefficients in real-time to extract features from audio recordings. Comprised of a Gaussian random matrix with elements updated through a least squares strategy following each frame, its filter order remains adaptable. The filter's performance is evaluated through its ability to reconstruct original audio signals, with results indicating its potential as a resilient feature extraction method. Furthermore, its efficiency is demonstrated through its reduced computational requirements, outperforming a comparable existing method while minimizing its impact on computational resources. The utility of this filter is explored in the context of its application in the audio spectrum, with preliminary findings suggesting its potential in the human speech spectrum, a range critical in the creation of robust feature sets for speech recognition systems. The human speech spectrum is particularly notable for its sensitivity to computational noise, a characteristic that may be mitigated by the proposed dynamic filter. The filter's ability to outperform traditional Gaussian windows in this context is demonstrated through its capacity to extract features from the LibriSpeech dataset, with results indicating its potential as a feature extraction method for robust speech recognition systems. The filter's performance is shown to be competitive with existing state-of-the-art methods in the field. The filter's code is publicly available through a GitHub repository. This relativistic modification affects the phase space for pair production and leads to a reduction in the cross section, particularly at low transverse momentum values. Specifically, we find that the modification factor for the charmonium production cross section at transverse momentum $p_T<2$ GeV is approximately $0.27\pm 0.05$, while for the bottomonium production cross section at $p_T<2$ GeV it is approximately $0.68\pm 0.13$. These results are consistent with theoretical expectations. Furthermore, we note that the charmonium production cross section is particularly sensitive to the threshold mass at which the binding energy of the charmonium pair is equal to the difference between the mass of the Higgs boson and the threshold mass of the quark-antiquark pair. This threshold mass is approximately 2.82 GeV for charmonium and 12.75 GeV for bottomonium. The Transformer model's computational costs can be extremely high due to its full attention mechanism. Researchers have developed sparse attention techniques to mitigate this issue by only considering relevant input data. However, these approaches often involve complex hyperparameters that affect model performance. Our proposed solution, gating dropout, provides an automated mechanism to regulate the interaction between input tokens by initially selecting unimportant tokens. This approach does not require adjustable parameters. We tested our gating dropout method in conjunction with sparse triggers and observed improved performance compared to manual pruning methods. Additionally, our gating dropout method outperforms dropout regularization on both sparse and full attention mechanisms. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art results in a multi-task Dutch language understanding task while significantly reducing computational costs. Our gating dropout method is an innovative tool for optimizing the trade-off between model performance and computational complexity. The associated code is available on GitHub.

The similarity is then used to determine the relative pose between two consecutive scans. This framework also allows for the consideration of subtle associations between entities and relations. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we create a new dataset based on a publicly available knowledge graph (DBpedia). Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over traditional link prediction methods, with our approach also showing improved performance when applied to other knowledge graphs. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the improved performance is primarily due to the learning of more abstract relations and a better understanding of entity and relation similarities. The development of effective and efficient monitoring methods is crucial for large-scale carbon capture and storage projects. Seismic data, particularly its ability to detect the formation of fluid interfaces, makes it an ideal monitoring approach. However, capturing high-quality pre- and post-injection seismic data is often hindered by logistical challenges. As a result, existing 4D seismic monitoring methods often rely on sparse data collected over long periods. This research introduces a novel, data-driven technique for 4D seismic monitoring that leverages a spatio-temporal convolutional neural network to track fluid interfaces without the need for simultaneous data collection. Instead, the model is trained on 3D images of pre-injection seismic data and simulated post-injection images, then applied to real-world data to predict the current state of large-scale storage facilities. This approach has been successfully demonstrated on a real-time data set from a large-scale storage project in Kansas, USA. Our results show that the method can accurately identify interfaces even in data collected prior to the fluid interface arrival, eliminating the need for simultaneous data collection. This approach has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of 4D seismic monitoring and facilitate widespread adoption of the technology. A novel approach called Federated Edge Computing has the potential to significantly enhance the efficiency of vehicle edge networks, particularly with the rapid increase in highly mobile connected vehicles. In this context, we propose an innovative method called Vehicular Edge Federated Training (VEFT) that efficiently utilizes edge resources and minimizes communication expenses in vehicle edge networks. VEFT first employs a clustering technique to group connected vehicles based on their edge resource availability, and then utilizes edge resources to train individual vehicles, model sharing, and federated gradient aggregation to update the global model. Furthermore, we present an optimization-based resource allocation framework that dynamically adjusts edge network resources based on traffic patterns and vehicle densities. The results of extensive simulations demonstrate the superiority of our approach in terms of model accuracy and vehicle resource utilization in vehicle edge networks. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the impact of vehicle density, vehicle connectivity, and vehicle mobility on the performance of vehicle edge networks. Most importantly, our study shows that vehicle edge federated training can provide comparable performance to centralized training methods even in highly mobile vehicle networks, paving the way for future research in federated learning and vehicle edge networks. Managing these interactions efficiently is a complex task, especially given the diverse range of devices and platforms involved. To address this challenge, our proposed architecture, known as the JADE Cloud InMemory Architecture (JCIMA), leverages cloud technology and in-memory computing to provide a scalable and persistent solution for managing interconnected digital entities. JCIMA employs a unique approach, where cloud technology and in-memory capabilities work in tandem to ensure high performance, increased scalability, and improved persistence. To evaluate the performance of JCIMA, we conducted a series of experiments using the Agent Platform Independent Infrastructure (API) and the Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents (FIPA) standards. Our results demonstrate JCIMA's ability to process high volumes of messages quickly and efficiently, achieving a response time of less than one second and a throughput of over 1000 messages per second. This performance surpasses existing solutions, which often rely on relational databases and require a significant amount of time to process messages. Our findings suggest that JCIMA is a promising candidate for supporting complex distributed applications, especially in the context of IoT and smart cities. It's found that nilpotent Lie groups corresponding to rank two have unique properties, with the solution to the matching problem being dependent on a specific algebraic surface S. Additionally, we establish that the Lie groups matching a given nilpotent Lie algebra are classified by a subset of points on S. We also provide explicit calculations for the Lie groups matching a given 2-step nilpotent Lie algebra, specifically those with a rank two nilpotent Lie algebra of Heisenberg type or Melikyan type. Moreover, we investigate the cohomology of the quotient space formed by these nilpotent Lie groups and provide an expression for the dimension of their respective central extensions. Finally, we utilize these findings to derive a Lie algebra structure on a manifold. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic led to a significant increase in syndromic monitoring research, with a focus on rapid disease detection. However, most of these methods were designed to identify a specific agent, such as SARS-CoV-2. Our study revisits the concept of non-specific syndromic monitoring, which aims to detect any potential outbreak by analyzing symptoms and conditions, rather than a particular disease. We developed and evaluated new methods for non-specific monitoring, using a wide range of data from various sources. Our results demonstrate that these approaches can effectively identify outbreaks earlier and with greater sensitivity than traditional methods, even when limited by available data. Our findings suggest that non-specific syndromic monitoring could be a valuable tool for outbreak detection and may help mitigate the limitations of agent-specific monitoring. We propose further research to integrate these approaches and improve overall outbreak detection capabilities. Handwritten date records are a widespread and time-consuming document type that require efficient processing. Date components consist of date symbols and spatial arrangements, along with potential punctuation marks and words. The complexity of handwritten texts further complicates date interpretation. Advanced techniques such as deep learning and transfer learning can be employed to improve date recognition. A novel, large-scale dataset for date recognition, DARE, containing 50,000 handwritten dates from over 2,500 writers, has been created with annotated components and properties. An end-to-end deep learning framework, DARE-Net, is proposed for date recognition, utilizing a two-stage approach with a spatial arrangement encoder and a date symbol encoder. The framework is trained with DARE and general text data, then fine-tuned using dates from various domains. Experiments on DARE and a public HASTA dataset show that DARE achieves state-of-the-art performance in date recognition. The DARE dataset and code are publicly available for research purposes. A demo version of the date recognition system can be accessed through a online demonstration. The source code for the demo system is also available. Effective learning of programming skills is linked to a range of cognitive processes, including both visual and mental abilities. To better understand how the brain processes these skills, researchers used functional magnetic resonance imaging to study the neural activity of 64 first-year students as they learned to code. A follow-up study with 20 participants using eye-tracking technology further explored the mechanisms behind their cognitive processes during this task. Our findings reveal a significant increase in brain activity specifically in areas associated with short-term memory, such as the prefrontal cortex and Wernicke's area, when students are given the option to read code information. Conversely, interactive tasks involving reading, visualizing, and coding with code editors decreases activity in these regions and increases activity in other areas associated with problem-solving, such as the intraparietal sulcus. Our study's findings have important implications for how programming should be taught and integrated into educational plans, and are particularly relevant for students who are new to the field. The issue of false discovery proportion (FDP) in multiple testing arises when a substantial number of false null hypotheses are incorrectly rejected. This paper examines the asymptotic reliability of several FDP estimators in dependent testing scenarios, specifically utilizing local polynomial regression and kernel smoothing techniques. Our findings indicate that these estimators can be unreliable in cases where the null hypotheses exhibit complex relationships, such as when the regression curves have sharp changes or can be represented using infinitely many parameters. This research provides a theoretical explanation for the unreliability of FDP estimators in real-world applications. Our results are demonstrated through simulations and a case study to further illustrate the importance of these findings. The research also identifies potential avenues for improving the asymptotic reliability of FDP estimators in future studies. Image dehazing is a critical image processing problem that affects the quality of captured images. The existing methods for image dehazing have several limitations, such as the inability to handle complex haze scenarios, poor performance in removing residual haze, and being computationally expensive. To address these limitations, a novel approach is proposed in this paper, termed as Efficient Dehazing via Rich Feature Extraction (EDRFE). EDRFE is a two-stage model that consists of a rich feature extraction module and a refinement module. The rich feature extraction module is designed to extract the detailed features of the haze map and the transmission map, while the refinement module is used to refine these features and produce a haze-free image. The refinement module is further divided into two sub-modules, a feature refinement module and a detail refinement module, which are trained with two different loss functions. To improve the performance of the haze removal, a Feature Affinity Module is introduced, which is used to calculate the feature affinity between the haze map and the transmission map. The results of the experiments show that EDRFE outperforms the existing methods for image dehazing in terms of both visual quality and performance metrics. As the intricacy and measurement scale of integrated circuits progress,
the coherence boundaries of modern computing systems become increasingly
restricted. This paper delves into the potential risks of manipulating
hardware coherence in interposer-based systems and the measures that can
be taken to counter them. We discovered that the advanced integration of
multiple cores on a single interposer enhances the potential for attacks
targeting data exchange data paths, and the elevated noise level in these
systems provides attackers with greater opportunities to execute them.
Furthermore, we found that the limitations of certain hardware components
make software-based countermeasures less effective. This paper showcases a
novel attack on interposer-based systems, utilizing a combination of
cache-side channel attacks and the exploitation of hardware coherence to
execute them. We also proposed a set of countermeasures, including the
implementation of a hardware-based coherence inspection mechanism and the
utilization of a software-based profiling tool to detect and prevent
coherence-based attacks. We successfully implemented and tested these
attacks and countermeasures on a real-world platform, and the results show
that the proposed attacks can be successfully executed and the proposed
countermeasures can effectively prevent them. This research contributes to
the development of a more secure computing environment by exposing the
vulnerabilities of modern computing systems and the measures that can be
taken to execute and prevent coherent attacks. Our findings are expected to
stimulate further research on the coherence-based attacks and countermeasures
in modern computing systems. The research materials, including the attack
code and additional information, are available at https://bit.ly/3BQqz1E.

We've developed a novel distributed learning approach called the Wellness Training Agency for Network Learning (WENT) that facilitates machine learning on large and diverse datasets by utilizing edge devices. WENT enables the utilization of edge devices as learning and computing resources to train models on large datasets by leveraging the combined resources of these devices. In this study, we successfully implemented WENT in an Android app and employed it to train a melanoma classification model using a dataset comprising 375 images. The results showed that the model we trained with WENT achieved a high classification accuracy of 96.44%, even after being tested on new, unseen data. Interestingly, our findings also indicated that the model trained with WENT performed comparably to a model trained on the entire dataset using a single GPU. Notably, this model achieved this performance while utilizing only 2% of the total dataset from our Android app users. WENT's ability to train machine learning models with high accuracy while minimizing data usage, and its portability across multiple devices, makes it a promising solution for distributed learning applications. We present a novel, single-pass YOLO-like algorithm for identifying sound events within audio recordings, a task known as sound event detection (SED). By drawing inspiration from YOLO's success in object detection for images, our approach leverages a U-Net-based encoder-decoder architecture for generating class-wise probability maps, which are then combined using a weighted sum to produce a single, overall probability map. This map is segmented into squares, and the highest probability pixel in each square is selected as the class label for that area. As a result, our algorithm can efficiently perform SED tasks within real-time constraints, achieving competitive performance on the FSD50K benchmark with relatively simple training and inference procedures. The mass of galaxy clusters is a key factor in cosmological research, but its accuracy is limited by various uncertainties. We then analyzed the properties of these clusters using the SZmassGen and GenClen codes and calculated their mass-to-temperature ratios. We combined the cluster data with observations from the Planck satellite and the HSC-SSP survey, then used the Monte Carlo EM algorithm to derive the posterior distribution of the cosmological parameters. Our findings indicate that the estimates of cosmological parameters are primarily affected by the scatter in the mass-temperature relation, with smaller impacts from the uncertainty in the SZ bias, hydrostatic equilibrium assumption, and cluster radius. Furthermore, we observed that the estimates of cosmological parameters are relatively insensitive to the specific properties used to calculate the cluster mass. Our results also indicate that the constraints on the cosmological parameters are limited by the sample size, with a need for at least 3000 clusters to accurately constrain the matter density and 8000 clusters to accurately constrain the equation of state of dark energy. Tangle 2.0 is a blockchain protocol that leverages a directed acyclic graph to facilitate decentralized consensus. Its core strength lies in being leaderless, but achieving consensus in this context poses a challenge. To address this issue, we introduce the Heaviest DAG (HDAG) concept within Tangle 2.0, which enables nodes to vote for the most reliable transactions on the network and ensure agreement through the creation of a new transaction on the heaviest path. This approach eliminates the need for a leader-based consensus method while maintaining the decentralized and fair properties of Tangle 2.0. Furthermore, the HDAG can be implemented using existing Tangle 2.0 components, resulting in a straightforward and efficient integration. Moreover, we demonstrate that this concept preserves the benefits of a leaderless Tangle 2.0, including improved security and fairness. In addition, we propose a simple algorithm to compute the heaviest DAG in Tangle 2.0, which can be implemented using a graph traversal approach. This algorithm has been tested through simulations, which demonstrate its effectiveness. Finally, we discuss the potential for further research opportunities in the context of Heaviest DAG for achieving consensus in Tangle 2.0. By integrating a hierarchical attention mechanism, RTFormer leverages both local and global contextual information while minimizing computational overhead. In this study, we examine how prior information influences the quantum search capabilities of Grover's algorithm in a setting of familiar and unknown spaces. We define an environment where an agent is aware of certain locations but not others and utilize a Prior Knowledge-based Quantum Search algorithm (PKQSG) that leverages this information to achieve a reduced number of queries. The PKQSG iteratively combines classical preprocessing steps with a single global quantum access to refine its search strategy. We demonstrate that this algorithm can solve Grover's problem in $\tilde{O}(s \cdot
\sqrt{\frac{L}{s}})$ queries when the unknown locations form a path within an $L$-long line and in $\tilde{O}(s \cdot
\sqrt{\frac{L}{s} + d})$ queries when the unknown locations are within a $d$-dimensional ball of diameter $d$. These results represent a 1/2 reduction in query complexity compared to the current, optimal PKGS algorithm and suggest that PKQSG could be a valuable tool for quantum exploration in a variety of environments. We also show that our findings cannot be easily extended to the Grover's search problem in a graph setting. Finally, we explore the broader implications of our research for quantum search and its potential applications in the real world. We also examine the effects on the axion-photon conversion process and the generation of a stochastic background of primordial axion photons. Our study reveals that ancient magnetic fields can significantly affect axion abundance, with some scenarios potentially conflicting with axion dark matter explanations for the cosmic microwave background's tilt anomaly. However, for axion dark matter candidates with larger axion-photon couplings, ancient magnetic fields may actually increase the axion abundance, making them more viable. Furthermore, we find that ancient magnetic fields can generate a stochastic background of primordial axion photons, potentially detectable by future CMB experiments. Specifically, for axions with a mass of 0.01 eV and a decay constant of 10^9 GeV, an axion-photon coupling of 10^-21 GeV^-1 would be sufficient to produce a background of 10^-5 GeV cm^-3, which could be detectable by CIBER, SIMBOLO, and other future experiments. In contrast, for axions with a decay constant of 10^12 GeV, the resulting background would be below the detection limits of these experiments. Our study also shows that ancient magnetic fields can potentially produce a primordial axion isocurvature perturbation, which could be detectable by future CMB experiments, although the impact on axion abundance is relatively minor in this case. Our study also emphasizes the need for future CMB experiments to detect a stochastic background of primordial axion photons, which could provide insight into the impact of ancient magnetic fields on axion abundance. Curriculum learning has been a successful method in semi-supervised learning, allowing models to progressively learn from increasingly complex data. However, achieving this is challenging due to the difficulty in pre-selecting high-quality data for model training. In contrast, our proposed approach, FlexMatch, utilizes a novel training strategy that combines a student-teacher framework with a dynamic approach to pseudo-labeling data. By leveraging a teacher model to generate high-quality pseudo-labels and a student model to train on them, our method enables efficient and accurate training of models. Specifically, our approach includes two key components: a student-teacher model pair and a dynamic pseudo-label threshold that adapts to the learning process. When the student model performs well, the teacher model is updated with a lower pseudo-label threshold, allowing for more accurate training. In contrast, our approach uses a higher pseudo-label threshold when the student model is still in the process of learning. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FlexMatch in semi-supervised learning, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple image classification tasks, including imageNet, CIFAR-100, and tiny imageNet. In this study, we have developed an approach to approximately solve the Schrodinger-Pauli equation in a time-varying magnetic field, particularly when the interaction is strong and rapidly changing, by drawing inspiration from quantum optics methods. Our method involves a diagonalization technique that uses a unitary transformation based on a time-varying multilevel system, which we have rigorously analyzed for its convergence and practical feasibility. We have applied this method to a specific scenario of a spin-$1/2$ particle experiencing a time-varying dipole interaction, resulting in a surprisingly simple and numerically stable solution that accurately captures key properties of the system. Our work paves the way for further research into diagonalization methods for more complex, strongly interacting systems in time-varying environments. We investigate the long-term behavior of quantum Markov chains in systems with infinite time periods, focusing on state spaces with a finite number of points. Our research reveals that when the transition dynamics are unitary, these chains form a unique equilibrium distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even when decoherence is present, these quantum Markov chains can still represent a stationary state, provided decoherence and unitarity have complementary effects. Notably, we show that when the decoherence process is unitary as well, these quantum Markov chains can be seen as the result of a quantum dynamics with a unique equilibrium point. Our findings are illustrated through numerical simulations of a two-level system experiencing decoherence. The implications of our results are significant and may be applied to model open quantum systems in quantum chemistry, solid-state physics, and quantum information. Federated learning, specifically customized federated learning (CFL), addresses the issue of differing sample distributions in different groups by tailoring the machine learning model to each specific group's needs. Traditional CFL methods, however, often require detailed prior knowledge of the data and may not be effective when the number of training samples is extremely limited. To address these challenges, we propose a novel CFL method called hypernet-consisted CFL (H-CFL), which utilizes hypernetworks to generate customized models for each group. Unlike previous methods, H-CFL does not require prior knowledge of the data and can be applied even with very small sample sizes. In our experiments, we demonstrated that H-CFL outperforms existing methods, even when the number of training samples increases, and even when the number of groups grows. Furthermore, we found that H-CFL can also be used to reduce computational costs by sharing model parameters across groups. To the best of our knowledge, our proposed method is the first to tackle CFL challenges in the context of extremely limited sample sizes and lack of detailed prior knowledge. As a result, H-CFL offers a more practical and efficient solution for real-world CFL applications. The code for H-CFL is publicly available on GitHub. Preconditioned eigensolvers are widely used in scientific and engineering applications. However, their convergence rates can be unpredictable and vary greatly depending on the specific problem being tackled. To address this limitation, we have developed a gradient optimization method that ensures geometric convergence for a broad range of preconditioned eigensolvers. By leveraging this approach, we have been able to derive convergence results for several standard methods, including the Lanczos, Lanczos-ADI, and conjugate gradient preconditioners. Furthermore, we have also established convergence bounds for these methods, which demonstrate that they achieve a geometric rate of convergence under specific conditions. In addition to our theoretical results, we have conducted numerical experiments to confirm the efficacy of our approach and validate its ability to provide accurate estimates of the convergence rate. Our work ultimately enables the development of more reliable preconditioned eigensolvers that achieve geometric convergence and can be applied to a wide range of problems. Notably, we have found that our approach can also be applied to more complex problems involving matrix pencils and linear complementarity problems. To address this issue, we propose a new method called Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Focus Network (DSTFocus), which anticipates accidents at an early stage. DSTFocus is a deep learning-based approach that effectively handles complex interactions between vehicles and environmental factors over time and space. It consists of a spatial-temporal attention module and a focus module, which work together to identify critical factors contributing to accidents. The spatial-temporal attention module enables the network to focus on key vehicles involved in potential accidents, while the focus module captures vehicle interactions and environmental influences. To optimize performance, we use a multi-task learning framework that includes a classification loss and an early anticipation loss. Experimental results on real-world traffic data demonstrate that DSTFocus significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving an improvement of 9.9% in anticipation accuracy and 5.9% in anticipation precision. Furthermore, our approach enables the visualization of the network's focus on key vehicles involved in potential accidents. Traditional question-answering systems typically provide answers accompanied by a single supporting statement. However, this approach can be limited, especially when multiple valid reasons exist for the answer. To address this limitation, we've developed a system that offers multiple supporting statements, ensuring they are both relevant and correct. Our approach relies on a new type of proof, called a chain of reasoning, which is derived from a large collection of truthfully formatted proofs. We present Entailer, a model-based meta-learner capable of generating these chains of reasoning. Experimentally, we've demonstrated that our approach produces more informative answers and is more accurate than existing question-answering techniques. Additionally, we've found that users prefer our approach and engage more with the provided evidence, indicating its potential to enhance the effectiveness of question-answering systems in real-world settings. Overall, our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the subcarrier correlation properties and phase noise, leading to the development of a new method that enhances detection performance. Our work paves the way for the creation of a low-cost, portable, and affordable device for diagnosing COVID-19 patients with respiratory insufficiency worldwide. We introduce a novel nonparametric test for conditional independence, utilizing localized data rearrangement techniques within the framework of the empirical process. This method is applied to both bivariate and multivariate scenarios, yielding statistical assessments for various functional relationships. Furthermore, we expand the localized rearrangement principle to investigate the conditional independence of multiple random variables. Through simulations, we demonstrate the test's reliability in detecting conditional independence under standard statistical models. In addition, we explore the local permutation test as a complementary approach for verifying conditional independence, complemented by an empirical evaluation of the test's performance in finite sample settings. Finally, we utilize the localized rearrangement test to investigate conditional independence within high-dimensional data sets derived from gene expression analysis of tumor subtypes. Specifically, we examine relationships between gene expression, tumor aggressiveness, and patient survival, drawing upon The Cancer Genome Atlas data. In this context, the localized rearrangement test proves effective in identifying conditional relationships between these variables, guided by theoretical interpretations. Secure programming languages rely on strong type systems to prevent security breaches, but they are weakened by typecast operations, which allow malicious code to bypass security restrictions. A typecast operation, though initially intended to handle exceptions, can be used to launch a type-based attack that bypasses even the most advanced type system. Due to the potential for such attacks, the development of typecast-safe secure programming languages has been hindered. 

We introduce Fuel, a compiler-based framework for secure memory management that addresses this challenge. Fuel is a type-system-independent solution that ensures the safe handling of typecasts in any programming language, effectively eliminating typecast-based attacks. 

Our evaluation of Fuel on various languages, including Rust, C, and Java, demonstrates its effectiveness in preventing typecast attacks. We have integrated Fuel into a software tool called CastFixer, which automatically modifies code to make it cast-safe, thereby facilitating the creation of secure software. Our results show that CastFixer can efficiently process large programs, even with thousands of typecast operations, in a short amount of time. We have also applied CastFixer to a real-world library, where it successfully eliminated typecast-based errors without introducing any performance overhead. Our research establishes that Fuel is a crucial component for creating secure software. Current solutions are often either too complex or provide suboptimal results due to their simplicity. To address this issue, we propose a new approach, Failure-Aware Semi-Centralized Virtual Network Embedding (FA-S-CVNE), which effectively manages FBDNs with multiple nodes. Our model leverages a unique failure-aware strategy to optimize virtual network embeddings, using a two-step optimization process that involves identifying optimal locations for virtual nodes and then selecting the best embedding pass. To further improve our approach, we integrate a novel failure probability estimation mechanism that takes into account the specific characteristics of each virtual node. By minimizing the number of network failures and reducing the complexity of the embedding process, our FA-S-CVNE model significantly outperforms existing methods in both real-world and simulation settings. The results demonstrate that our approach can lead to substantial cost savings and enhanced service quality for both virtual and physical networks. Specifically, our model outperforms state-of-the-art CVNE and VNE approaches, achieving an average reduction of 24.2% in network failures and 16.6% in embedding complexity. Although user interaction is vital for shaping personal preferences and providing a personalized experience, there has been a lack of research on the underlying factors influencing user engagement. For many individuals, Google Calendar serves as a central tool to organize and plan their daily activities. In this study, we present the outcome of a "Google Calendar Challenge" - a research initiative where participants manually log their activities over a month using Google Calendar. The resulting dataset comprises over 22,000 annotated entries, enabling us to examine the diverse nature of everyday tasks. Notably, we've found that less than 3% of daily tasks remain private, whereas the majority fall under the categories of work, leisure, and social activities. Furthermore, we've identified a set of recurring time patterns that are often overlooked in time-use research, including the common occurrence of morning routines, sleep patterns, and specific time intervals dedicated to meals. Additionally, we've analyzed the duration and timing of tasks, revealing that most last around 30 minutes to one hour and typically commence between two and three hours past wake-up time. Our findings also suggest a daily routine of work, leisure, and rest. The "Google Calendar Challenge" offers an innovative method for collecting data on daily activities and provides valuable insights into time-use research. We propose that researchers can replicate and build upon this approach to gain a deeper understanding of people's daily habits and routines. Detailed instructions on how to participate in the "Google Calendar Challenge" are available online. All the data collected from participants is also publicly accessible, allowing others to explore the dataset and build upon our research. In this research, we investigate the properties of the Faddeev-Popov gauge fixing procedure within the context of pure gauge Quantum Electrodynamics. Specifically, we examine the influence of this procedure on the Schwinger function, which represents the correlation between gauge-invariant fields. Notably, we find that the Faddeev-Popov gauge fixing introduces a divergence in the Schwinger function, leading to a violation of positivity for Wilson loops in pure gauge QED. Linear regression is a foundational statistical tool, yet its predictive model lacks essential flexibility to account for non-linear relationships in data. This limitation becomes apparent when analyzing real-world data, which often exhibits non-linear patterns, forcing practitioners to employ non-linear transformation techniques to capture these patterns effectively. In this context, we investigate the concept of predictive model flexibility in linear regression, deriving a mathematical expression for it and examining its relationship with parametric models. Our analysis reveals that flexible location-scale models can replicate any non-linear relationship, effectively incorporating all relevant information. However, we also find that introducing additional complexity may compromise the model's interpretability. Notably, our results validate the effectiveness of a recently proposed non-linear transformation model, the Box-Cox-Normal, in capturing non-linear relationships while maintaining interpretability. To illustrate these findings, we present a case study using both simulated data and real-world weather data from the UK's Met Office. Our research has practical implications for data analysts, who can now leverage our results to inform their model selection process and enhance their models for real-world applications. Finally, we discuss the broader applications of our work, including its potential to generalize beyond traditional linear regression models. Personal prediction involves making forecasts tailored to an individual, as opposed to a group. It differs from traditional prediction methods, which often focus on group averages. Research has shown that personal predictions can be more accurate and beneficial in various settings. Yet, the trade-offs associated with this approach are not well understood. To address this knowledge gap, we explore the trade-offs of personal prediction through three primary lenses: privacy, fairness, and utility. We analyze how personal prediction affects these aspects, both theoretically and empirically. Our findings reveal that personal prediction can compromise both fairness and utility when not managed properly. However, we discovered that it may offer a balance of privacy, fairness, and utility under certain conditions. To validate our conclusions, we conducted a series of experiments across various domains. Our study contributes to the growing literature on personal prediction by highlighting its trade-offs and providing a framework for mitigating them in real-world applications. Our findings reveal that the promise abstraction consistently yields predictable outcomes in scenarios with shared state and visibility issues, aligning with existing research on the subject. Moreover, our event structure-based approach provides a unified framework for analyzing the behavior of computations under various memory models. We examine a type of free boundary problem where a diffusion process is confined to a half-plane and can spread into a two-dimensional space. In this scenario, the diffusion front creates its own boundary, beyond which the process does not advance. Our findings demonstrate that the free boundary problem exhibits similarities with the classic obstacle problem, provided the free boundary is treated as a distinct entity. Using the concept of a viscosity level, we derive similarity conditions for the free boundary and an equivalent formulation of the problem, focusing on the characteristics of the diffusion process and the behavior of its extension into the two-dimensional space. This new formulation can be employed to develop numerical methods for solving the problem. We also prove the existence of solutions to the free boundary problem, building upon the well-established theory of the obstacle problem, and illustrate our results with numerical examples. Furthermore, we show that the free boundary problem can be transformed into a nonlinear integro-differential equation, whose solutions converge to those of the original problem as the nonlinear coefficient tends towards zero. This convergence is demonstrated through numerical examples. We also explore the possibility of small-time explosion in the free boundary problem, a phenomenon analogous to explosion in the classic obstacle problem, and propose a modification to the problem that prevents explosion while approximating the original problem. This modification is shown to be stable. The paper concludes with a numerical comparison between the original problem and its modified version. The results indicate that the modifications have a negligible impact on the solutions. We have made the numerical code used in this paper available online. Go, a popular open-source programming language, has become widely used for
developing distributed systems and cloud-native applications. However, Go's
concurrency model can sometimes lead to bugs that are difficult to detect. 
To address this issue, we introduce BinGo, a static analysis tool for Go code.
By converting source code into intermediate representations, BinGo identifies
potential errors using a combination of pattern recognition and data flow
analysis. Our study found that BinGo effectively detects most concurrency issues
in popular open-source and commercial Go programs, and in fact outperforms
existing static analysis tools. Additionally, we have successfully used BinGo
to identify previously unknown bugs in well-known Go libraries, and our
methodology demonstrates its feasibility in real-world applications.

Overall, our results indicate that equiformer offers a more effective way to model 3D relationships in proteins compared to other approaches. A major challenge in autonomous driving and mobile robotics involves accurately predicting the future movements of other agents. Although many advanced algorithms have been developed, they often struggle when dealing with complex and unpredictable scenarios. To address this limitation, we're exploring a new approach called Multi-Scenario Trajectory Prediction (MSTP), which generates multiple hypothetical future scenarios for an agent's behavior. By combining these scenarios, we can create a more accurate forecast of what might happen next. Our proposed method draws inspiration from the concept of the branching paths of time from science fiction, which suggests that the future is not fixed and can be predicted using different scenarios. In our approach, we use a GAN-based architecture to generate these hypothetical scenarios, and then use a decision-making module to select the most likely course of events. Our experiments show that MSTP outperforms traditional single-scenario prediction methods, especially when dealing with complex and unpredictable scenarios. Furthermore, we've developed a new dataset called TrajectC: a collection of real-world data that showcases various unpredictable scenarios, which can be used to train and test our proposed method. Our code and data are now publicly available for others to use and build upon. As we look to the future, we're excited to see how our proposed method can be used to better predict human behavior and improve safety in autonomous driving and mobile robotics. This research focuses on developing a theoretical framework for non-log-concave sampling. Key contributions include novel first-order stationarity guarantees for Langevin Monte Carlo methods. In particular, under specified conditions, we show that the sequence of invariant measures generated by the Markov Chain can be compactly represented within a defined ball centered around the initial data. Furthermore, we establish that the sequence converges to a uniform distribution within this ball. These results are based on a novel concept called near-stationarity, which we define and demonstrate to be equivalent to uniform distribution within the ball. Additionally, we show that the Markov Chain reaches first-order stationarity in finite time with high probability. The key factor enabling these results is the near-stationarity concept, which differs from log-concavity by allowing for more flexible energy functions. Ultimately, our research paves the way for further advancements in non-log-concave sampling theory. Quantum computing holds great promise in tackling complex problems, particularly in optimizing molecular interactions. To achieve this, researchers have been exploring the application of quantum algorithms in drug discovery. In this study, we developed a universal, programmable Gaussian Boson generator and successfully implemented it in a quantum simulation of the Lindblad master equation to simulate temperature-dependent enzyme inhibition. By utilizing this generator, we simulated the binding dynamics of a small molecule with its target enzyme, revealing the impact of temperature on binding kinetics. Our findings suggest that the binding process can be significantly accelerated at higher temperatures, which may inform the development of new drugs. To validate our results, we also examined the quantum simulation of a real-world system, namely the tryptophan synthetase-tryptophan complex. Our study demonstrates the potential of Gaussian Boson generators in quantum simulations, particularly in drug discovery applications. With further advancements, this technology may enable the in-depth analysis of temperature-dependent binding dynamics in various molecular systems. The findings from this study may contribute to the discovery of novel therapeutic agents and contribute to the advancement of precision medicine. Automated evaluation techniques for analyzing cellular electron microscopy (EM) have been developed to efficiently process the vast amounts of data generated by the field. This research area has been expanding rapidly over the past decade, driven by advancements in data collection and computing capabilities. This paper provides an overview of the current state of automated image processing in EM, covering various applications, evaluation methods, and performance metrics. Additionally, it discusses key challenges and offers guidance for new researchers entering the field. The objectives of this review are multi-faceted: firstly, it aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the methods for assessing the quality of EM images; secondly, it highlights the broader applications of these methods, such as segmentation, registration, and registration-based denoising; and thirdly, it identifies areas for future investigation. The review draws on over 200 recent publications and 100 high-quality, citable references to provide a thorough review of the methods for evaluating EM images. The code and data used for this review are publicly available, allowing for replication and extension of the methods discussed. The current review focuses on automated image assessment methods, but future work could expand the scope to include other EM-related tasks, such as segmentation, registration, and denoising. The authors of this review are aware that they may have inadvertently overlooked some relevant publications and would appreciate any feedback or correction. They look forward to contributing to the advancement of the methods for evaluating EM images and exploring the broader applications of these methods in the field. The way in which web applications interact with data across different domains is a crucial aspect of web security. Despite advancements in recent years, web APIs have continued to evolve to enable the cross-scope sharing of data. This ongoing development has resulted in a multitude of mechanisms, making it challenging for developers and researchers to accurately assess and analyze web applications and identify potential security vulnerabilities. To address this issue, we propose a systematic framework for categorizing cross-scope data transfer mechanisms, which provides a clear understanding and standardization of existing and emerging web protocols. This framework offers a structured approach to tracking changes in web technology, facilitates the evaluation of web security and privacy implications, and enables the development of automated tools for vulnerability detection. We have applied our framework to analyze the history of cross-scope data transfer in web APIs, demonstrating its practical application and effectiveness. Furthermore, we have used our framework to develop a static analysis tool that identifies cross-origin reflected attacks in web applications, as demonstrated on a real-world dataset. This paper serves as a foundation for further research on the evaluation and analysis of web security and the development of new protocols. The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly disrupted the normal progression of scientific research, leading to a substantial backlog of studies that were initially planned for immediate publication. To better understand the impact of the pandemic on scientific productivity in life sciences, we analyzed a vast database of publications from PubMed that contain estimated publication dates. Our analysis reveals that the pandemic triggered a pause in ongoing research, particularly in the fields of biomedical research and clinical trials. We found that the majority of paused studies were in the stages of clinical trials, and interestingly, the most critical areas of research in the life sciences were among those most affected. Our study also shows that the pandemic led to an increase in research productivity in the following months, indicating that the pause in ongoing research was quickly filled by new studies. Overall, our research suggests that the pandemic led to a temporary pause in paused research and an acceleration of research productivity in the following months. Our findings have significant implications for how research should be planned and managed in light of future global health crises. Hydrogen-rich crystals exhibit exceptional sensitivity in detecting low-mass weakly interacting sub-GeV dark matter particles. This sensitivity arises from the enhanced cross-section of interactions between these particles and the abundant protons within the crystal. Our research focuses on the principles and practical limitations of using hydrogen-rich crystals in direct detection experiments, with a specific emphasis on superconducting tunnel junction detectors. We present the design of a new detector system, the Cryogenic H2-Dark Matter (CHDM) experiment, which leverages sapphire crystals and high-sensitivity transition-edge sensors. CHDM aims to achieve a superior sensitivity in the low-mass dark matter regime, with a projected detection threshold of 10^-44 pb/arbitrary coupling strength at 50 eV. This achievement will position CHDM as the most sensitive dark matter experiment to date for masses below 50 eV. CHDM is also designed to be highly sensitive to dark matter particles with masses between 1-10 eV. This is made possible by its ability to detect events with energies as low as 20 meV. Our research also highlights the importance of incorporating data analysis techniques that account for the statistical fluctuations inherent in the detector's response. This is crucial for accurately distinguishing between signal and noise events within the detector's energy spectrum. Foundation models, a new category of trained machine learning models, have garnered significant attention for their ability to tackle complex tasks. Despite this interest, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding the creation and potential impacts of these models. This article seeks to fill that gap by examining the current wave of foundation models through a historical and interdisciplinary lens, drawing upon the creation narratives of early natural language processing models. By doing so, it aims to shed light on the underlying assumptions and potential limitations of foundation models, particularly those related to their scalability and potential to drive technological advancements. Additionally, this study identifies areas of overlap between foundation models and cognitive science models, and discusses the need for more research into the social and cultural implications of these models, as well as their potential effects on human work and society. Ultimately, this article aims to encourage a more critical and nuanced approach to the development and deployment of foundation models. This paper investigates mixed graphs that possess a single minimal vertex with two positive eigenvalues. Such graphs are found to have a specific structural configuration in two distinct cases. Either the minimal vertex is part of a cycle that includes all other vertices, or it forms part of a directed cycle that includes all other pairs of vertices, assuming the minimal vertex has a degree of two. Additionally, we have identified a mixed graph with five vertices that possesses exactly two positive eigenvalues and does not satisfy either of these characteristics. This graph is characterized as having a directed triangle that includes an undirected edge, and an undirected edge connected to the opposite edge of the directed triangle. Similarly, we have determined that any mixed graph with six or more vertices that possesses exactly two positive eigenvalues can be constructed by adding either a new pair of edges to the minimal vertex or adding a new pair of directed edges to the minimal vertex, provided that the minimal vertex has a degree of two. Finally, we have established that there are no mixed graphs with seven or more vertices that possess exactly two positive eigenvalues and have a minimal vertex with a degree greater than two. This was achieved by showing that any mixed graph with seven or more vertices that possesses exactly two positive eigenvalues can be reduced to the configuration of a directed cycle with an undirected edge, and an undirected path. This reduction was accomplished by removing the undirected edges from the minimal vertex and reconstructing the graph. Notably, we have found that the minimal vertex has a degree of two in this new configuration. This result implies that the minimal vertex has a degree of two in all mixed graphs with exactly two positive eigenvalues and seven or more vertices. This result is in contrast to the situation in simple graphs, where the minimal vertex with two positive eigenvalues and seven or more vertices can have a degree of three. This difference highlights a key distinction between the spectral properties of mixed and simple graphs. This difference is further illustrated by considering the graphs with exactly two positive eigenvalues and ten or more vertices. This case is more complex, and we have found that the minimal vertex has a degree of three if and only if the graph has a specific configuration. Neural network attribution methods are assessed through two key characteristics: 
stability and consistency. Although consistency has garnered more attention in 
recent studies, stability has traditionally been the more stringent of the two. 
However, this paper presents a novel framework for examining attribution 
stability and reveals that it's actually less restrictive than the commonly 
adopted definition. Furthermore, we establish that attribution methods 
currently being developed are more resilient to network weight perturbations in 
terms of stability but less so in terms of consistency. Our analysis also shows 
that the widely used L1 norm for attribution measurement can be less stable than 
others, whereas higher-norm attributions tend to be more consistent. To 
understand these relationships better, we also introduce a method for visualizing 
the interplay between attribution measurement and stability, offering a more 
comprehensive understanding of attribution methods. Our empirical findings are 
backed by theoretical analysis, and we hope that this work will facilitate the 
development of attribution methods that are both consistent and stable. 
Ultimately, our goal is to accelerate the creation of attribution methods that 
provide accurate explanations for complex predictions. The code for our research 
is available on https://github.com/InteractML/Attribution-Stability-Analysis.

This note provides new, sharp lower bounds for the depth of $I^2$ based on
known limits for the depth and Cohen-Macaulay property of edge ideals in
graphs. Our results specifically improve a previous finding by Herzog and Hibi. \newline
Given a graph G, we demonstrate that its corresponding edge ideal $I(G)$
has depth at least $n-G\setminus K_n$ on a n-nodal graph G with the property
that removing any vertex and all its connected edges results in a connected graph. 
This improved bound is also shown to be tight for complete bipartite graphs. \newline
Furthermore, we establish that if the depth of $I(G)^2$ is greater than or equal to the depth of $I(G\setminus \{v\})^2$, then $I(G)$ has depth greater than or equal to the depth of $I(G\setminus \{v\})$. 
This result is then applied to graphs G with the property that removing any vertex and all its connected edges results in a connected graph.

The field of open-set identification addresses the challenge of recognizing when an input falls outside known classes. This issue is significant in real-world scenarios where data often contains unknown or novel instances. Most existing approaches to open-set identification are based on the premise that training and testing data share the same distribution. However, when the distribution changes between training and testing phases, these methods often struggle to detect out-of-distribution inputs. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach that leverages similarity learning to develop a more robust open-set identification method. Our approach involves generating diverse, synthetic examples from a single input and then learning a similarity function that distinguishes in-distribution from out-of-distribution data. This novel method is capable of adapting to changing data distributions and performing well across a wide range of scenarios. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and MNIST. Our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both accuracy and robustness to distribution shifts. We also provide code for our method on https://github.com/zhzytex/os-i. Additionally, we release a new benchmark for open-set identification and report our results, along with those of other leading methods. The benchmark can be found at https://os-benchmark.github.io.
